case: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of dark brown urine and puffy eyelids for 2 days. Three weeks ago he had crusted, honey-colored sores on the anteromedial surfaces of both lower legs that were not treated. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 134/88 mm Hg (above the 95th percentile for age). Examination shows periorbital edema, 1+ pitting edema of the ankles, and healing crusted lesions on both shins. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood, 1+ protein, and red blood cell casts. Serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL (0.3 to 0.7). Serum C3 is 38 mg/dL (90 to 180), and C4 is 24 mg/dL (10 to 40). The antistreptolysin O titer is within the reference range, and the anti-DNase B titer is elevated. Diagnosis: poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis after impetigo.

questions.stem: Over the next 3 days his serum creatinine rises to 1.6 mg/dL, and a renal biopsy is performed. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane
Mesangial IgA deposits with mesangial proliferation
Subepithelial humps with granular IgG and C3
Subendothelial wire loops with full-house staining
approach: Recognize nephritic syndrome 1 to 4 weeks after a group A streptococcal skin infection with low C3.
Recall that this is a type III reaction in which immune complexes form in or deposit on the glomerulus.
Match the disease to its biopsy picture: lumpy subepithelial deposits on electron microscopy and granular staining on immunofluorescence.
questions.why: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type III hypersensitivity reaction. Streptococcal antigens lodge in the glomerulus, antibodies bind them, and complement is activated, drawing in neutrophils and causing a diffusely hypercellular glomerulus. Electron microscopy shows dense subepithelial humps on the outer side of the basement membrane. Immunofluorescence shows granular, lumpy-bumpy deposits of IgG and C3. Skin infections favor a rise in anti-DNase B, while the ASO titer often stays low after impetigo.
whyNot: Linear IgG outlining the basement membrane is the pattern of anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome), a type II reaction against collagen IV. It would fit a young adult with hemoptysis and nephritis.
Mesangial IgA is IgA nephropathy, which causes hematuria within 1 to 2 days of a mucosal infection with normal C3. His 3-week delay and low C3 point away from it.
Correct.
Wire loops with IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q (full-house) are typical of diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis, which lowers both C3 and C4.

questions.stem: Which of the following initiating events best explains why his C3 is low while his C4 remains normal?
options: C3b binding factor B on bacterial antigens
C1q binding to IgG in circulating immune complexes
Mannose-binding lectin binding to bacterial sugars
C1 inhibitor deficiency with unchecked C1 activity
approach: Note the pattern: C3 low, C4 normal.
Recall that the classical and lectin pathways both cleave C4 to build C4b2a, while the alternative pathway builds C3bBb without C4.
Conclude that the alternative pathway is doing most of the consuming.
questions.why: All three complement pathways converge on a C3 convertase. The classical pathway (C1q binding IgG or IgM complexes) and the lectin pathway (mannose-binding lectin on microbial sugars) both cleave C4 and C2 to make C4b2a. The alternative pathway starts with slow spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 (tickover); on a surface that lacks regulators, C3b binds factor B, factor D cleaves it, and C3bBb amplifies itself. Streptococcal antigens in the glomerulus favor this loop, so C3 is used up and C4 is spared.
whyNot: Correct.
C1q binding starts the classical pathway, in which C1s cleaves C4 and C2. That route would consume C4 along with C3, as in active lupus.
The lectin pathway uses MBL-associated serine proteases that cleave C4 and C2, just like C1s. It would also lower C4.
Without C1 inhibitor, C1 keeps cleaving C4, so C4 falls while C3 stays normal. That is hereditary angioedema, the opposite pattern.

questions.stem: During the skin infection 3 weeks earlier, which group of lymph nodes was most likely to have been enlarged and tender?
options: Popliteal nodes in the fat of the popliteal fossa
Epitrochlear nodes above the medial elbow
Internal iliac nodes along the pelvic wall
Vertical group of superficial inguinal nodes
approach: Place the lesions: the anteromedial lower legs.
Recall that superficial lymph vessels from the medial foot and anteromedial leg follow the great saphenous vein.
Follow those vessels to the vertical group of superficial inguinal nodes near the saphenous opening.
questions.why: Superficial lymph from most of the lower limb, including the anteromedial leg and medial foot, travels with the great saphenous vein to the vertical (inferior) group of superficial inguinal nodes. These nodes then drain to the deep inguinal and external iliac nodes. Only the lateral foot and posterolateral calf, which drain with the small saphenous vein, go first to the popliteal nodes. Tender inguinal nodes are a common finding with impetigo or cellulitis of the shin.
whyNot: Popliteal nodes receive superficial lymph that runs with the small saphenous vein from the lateral foot and the back of the calf. Lesions on the front and inner shin drain elsewhere.
Epitrochlear nodes drain the ulnar side of the hand and forearm. They would enlarge with an infection of the little finger, for example.
Internal iliac nodes drain pelvic organs, the deep perineum, and the gluteal region. They are not palpable and do not receive superficial lymph from the leg.
Correct.

topics: Lymphatic drainage of the lower limb

questions.stem: Twelve weeks later his urine has cleared of red cell casts and his blood pressure is normal. Which of the following serum complement results is most likely at this visit?
options: C3 decreased, C4 decreased
C3 normal, C4 normal
C3 decreased, C4 normal
C3 normal, C4 decreased
approach: Recall the expected course: C3 falls during the first weeks and returns to normal within about 6 to 8 weeks.
Note that his clinical findings have resolved by 12 weeks.
Use the rule that persistently low C3 suggests another diagnosis.
questions.why: In poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, C3 is low in almost every child during the acute phase and returns to normal within about 6 to 8 weeks, along with clinical recovery. C4 stays normal throughout. A C3 that remains low past 8 weeks is a red flag for C3 glomerulopathy, membranoproliferative disease, or lupus. Reading complement this way helps sort nephritis: low C3 and C4 in active SLE, low C3 alone in poststreptococcal disease, and low C4 alone in hereditary angioedema.
whyNot: Low C3 and low C4 together signal classical pathway consumption, as in active lupus nephritis. It would not fit a patient whose nephritis is resolving.
Correct.
This is the pattern during the acute illness. If C3 stayed low beyond about 8 weeks, the diagnosis should be reconsidered, for example C3 glomerulopathy or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
Normal C3 with low C4 is the pattern of hereditary angioedema, in which C1 inhibitor deficiency lets C1 consume C4.

case: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue and three skin infections over the past 4 months. She has a 9-year history of rheumatoid arthritis treated irregularly. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Examination shows symmetric swelling of the metacarpophalangeal, proximal interphalangeal, and wrist joints with ulnar deviation of the fingers, firm nontender nodules over the extensor forearms, and a spleen palpable 5 cm below the left costal margin. Hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL (12 to 16), leukocyte count is 2,600/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000) with an absolute neutrophil count of 700/mm3 (1,500 to 8,000), and platelet count is 210,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000). Rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are positive. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 58 mm/h (0 to 30). Diagnosis: rheumatoid arthritis with Felty syndrome.

questions.stem: Radiographs of her hands are most likely to show which of the following?
options: Marginal MCP and wrist erosions sparing the DIP joints
DIP osteophytes with subchondral sclerosis and joint space loss
DIP erosions with pencil-in-cup deformity and periostitis
Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges near tophi
approach: Recognize seropositive, symmetric small joint arthritis with nodules as rheumatoid arthritis.
Recall that synovial pannus erodes bone first at the bare areas at the joint margins.
Apply the joint distribution: MCP, PIP, and wrist involved, DIP spared.
questions.why: In rheumatoid arthritis, inflamed synovium proliferates into a pannus of fibroblasts, macrophages, and lymphocytes. Pannus secretes enzymes and RANKL, which activates osteoclasts at the joint margins where bone is not covered by cartilage. Radiographs show periarticular osteopenia, symmetric joint space narrowing, and marginal erosions of the MCP, PIP, and wrist joints, with the DIP joints typically spared. Felty syndrome is the triad of rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly, and neutropenia, usually in long-standing seropositive disease.
whyNot: Correct.
Osteophytes and sclerosis at the DIP joints (Heberden nodes) are osteoarthritis, a wear-and-tear disease without synovial pannus or autoantibodies.
Pencil-in-cup DIP erosions with new bone formation are typical of psoriatic arthritis, which is seronegative and often asymmetric.
Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges beside soft tissue tophi are chronic gout, caused by urate crystal deposits.

questions.stem: Testing of her HLA genotype is most likely to show which of the following susceptibility alleles and functions?
options: HLA-DR2, presenting myelin peptides to CD4 T cells
HLA-DQ2, presenting deamidated gliadin to CD4 T cells
HLA-DR3, presenting pancreatic islet cell peptides to CD4 T cells
HLA-DR4, presenting citrullinated peptides to CD4 T cells
approach: Note the anti-CCP antibodies: her immune response targets citrullinated proteins.
Recall that HLA-DR4 alleles carrying the shared epitope bind citrullinated peptides well.
Connect class II presentation to CD4 T cell help for the B cells that make anti-CCP.
questions.why: Seropositive rheumatoid arthritis is strongly associated with HLA-DR4 (HLA-DRB1 alleles with the shared epitope). Inflammation and smoking increase citrullination, the conversion of arginine to citrulline by peptidylarginine deiminase. The shared epitope pocket binds citrullinated peptides tightly, so CD4 T cells respond and help B cells make anti-CCP antibodies. Anti-CCP is the most specific serologic test for rheumatoid arthritis.
whyNot: HLA-DR2 is linked to multiple sclerosis and Goodpasture syndrome. It is not the main risk allele for seropositive rheumatoid arthritis.
HLA-DQ2 (and DQ8) present gluten peptides modified by tissue transglutaminase in celiac disease.
HLA-DR3 and DR4 together raise the risk of type 1 diabetes, where T cells attack pancreatic beta cells. DR3 is not the rheumatoid arthritis allele.
Correct.

questions.stem: Additional studies show serum iron of 35 µg/dL (50 to 170), total iron-binding capacity of 210 µg/dL (250 to 400), and ferritin of 380 ng/mL (12 to 150). Which of the following best explains the low serum iron despite high ferritin?
options: Transferrin induction by IL-1, binding free serum iron
Hepcidin induction by IL-6, trapping iron in macrophages
Ferroportin induction by TNF-alpha, raising iron export
Haptoglobin induction by IL-6, binding iron after hemolysis
approach: Recognize the pattern of anemia of chronic disease: low iron, low TIBC, high ferritin.
Recall that IL-6 makes the liver produce hepcidin as part of the acute phase response.
Apply hepcidin's action: it degrades ferroportin, trapping iron in macrophages and enterocytes.
questions.why: Chronic inflammation drives the acute phase response. IL-6 is the main signal telling hepatocytes to make hepcidin, along with CRP, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A, and ferritin. Hepcidin binds ferroportin, the only iron exporter, and causes it to be internalized and degraded. Iron stays locked in macrophages and duodenal cells, so serum iron falls even though stores (ferritin) are high. This anemia of chronic disease likely adds to her low hemoglobin along with splenic sequestration.
whyNot: Transferrin is a negative acute phase protein. Inflammation lowers it, which is why her iron-binding capacity is low.
Correct.
More ferroportin would release iron into plasma and raise serum iron. In inflammation, ferroportin is removed from the cell surface.
Haptoglobin is an acute phase protein, but it binds free hemoglobin. It does not control serum iron.

questions.stem: Her neutropenia results partly from removal of antibody-coated neutrophils in her enlarged spleen. In which splenic compartment are these coated cells mainly engulfed by macrophages?
options: Periarteriolar lymphoid sheath
Germinal centers of the white pulp
Splenic cords of the red pulp
Trabecular veins
approach: Identify the target: IgG-coated blood cells that must be filtered out of circulating blood.
Recall that in the open circulation, blood is released into the splenic cords, which are packed with macrophages.
Choose the red pulp cords as the site where opsonized cells are removed.
questions.why: Splenic red pulp is made of the cords of Billroth and the venous sinusoids. Blood from penicillar arterioles empties into the cords, a loose meshwork full of macrophages, and must squeeze through slits in the sinusoid walls to return to the circulation. Macrophages in the cords use Fc receptors to grab IgG-coated cells, which is how the spleen clears antibody-coated neutrophils in Felty syndrome and antibody-coated red cells in warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The white pulp (T cell sheath, B cell follicles, marginal zone) handles immune responses to blood-borne antigens.
whyNot: The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath is the T cell zone of the white pulp, wrapped around the central arteriole. It is not the main site for filtering blood cells.
Germinal centers are where activated B cells proliferate and undergo affinity maturation, within white pulp follicles.
Correct.
Trabecular veins carry blood that has already passed through the red pulp out toward the splenic vein. They are lined by endothelium with no filtering macrophages.

topics: Fc receptor clearance in the spleen

case: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of dry cough, shortness of breath on exertion, and painful red eyes. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. Examination shows tender red nodules on both shins and ciliary flush with inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber of both eyes. A chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with reticular opacities in both upper lobes. Serum calcium is 11.9 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), parathyroid hormone is 9 pg/mL (10 to 65), and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is 92 pg/mL (18 to 72). Transbronchial biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas, and stains for acid-fast bacilli and fungi are negative. Diagnosis: pulmonary sarcoidosis with hypercalcemia.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional laboratory findings is most likely?
options: Elevated serum parathyroid hormone-related peptide
Positive cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies
Positive interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis
Elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme activity
approach: Pull together the findings: hilar adenopathy, uveitis, erythema nodosum, noncaseating granulomas.
Name the disease: sarcoidosis.
Recall that epithelioid cells in sarcoid granulomas secrete angiotensin-converting enzyme.
questions.why: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem disease of noncaseating granulomas, most often in the lungs and hilar nodes. Other common sites are the eyes (anterior uveitis), skin (erythema nodosum), and salivary glands. Epithelioid macrophages in the granulomas produce angiotensin-converting enzyme, so serum ACE is elevated in many patients and roughly tracks the total granuloma burden. Lofgren syndrome, an acute form with erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar adenopathy, and ankle arthritis, usually resolves on its own.
whyNot: PTH-related peptide causes hypercalcemia with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. It would not raise 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D or produce noncaseating granulomas.
c-ANCA points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which causes necrotizing granulomas and vasculitis of the airways and kidneys.
A positive assay would suggest tuberculosis, which forms caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli. Her stains were negative, and sarcoidosis often blunts T cell responses to tuberculin.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her hypercalcemia?
options: Hepatic 25-hydroxylase increased by inflammation
Macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase escaping PTH control
Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase stimulated by PTH
Macrophage 24-hydroxylase deficiency slowing calcitriol breakdown
approach: Note high calcium with suppressed PTH and high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
Conclude that calcitriol is being made outside the kidney's normal feedback loop.
Recall that activated granuloma macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase driven by IFN-gamma, without PTH control.
questions.why: Normally the kidney's 1-alpha-hydroxylase is switched on by PTH and low phosphate and switched off by calcitriol and high calcium. In sarcoidosis, IFN-gamma activated macrophages in the granulomas express their own 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which ignores these signals. They convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol, which raises intestinal calcium absorption and causes hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria while PTH is suppressed. Inside macrophages, calcitriol also induces the antimicrobial peptide cathelicidin, part of normal innate defense.
whyNot: Hepatic 25-hydroxylation is loosely regulated and only makes the storage form, 25-hydroxyvitamin D. It does not produce active calcitriol.
Correct.
Her PTH is suppressed, so the kidney's 1-alpha-hydroxylase is turned down. The calcitriol must come from another source.
A lack of 24-hydroxylase raises calcitriol in a rare inherited hypercalcemia of infancy. It is not the mechanism in granulomatous disease.

questions.stem: The granulomas consist of tight clusters of epithelioid macrophages and multinucleated giant cells. Which of the following signals most directly converts macrophages into these cells?
options: Interferon-gamma from Th1 CD4 T cells
Interleukin-4 from Th2 CD4 T cells
Interleukin-17 from Th17 CD4 T cells
Interleukin-10 from regulatory T cells
approach: Recognize the granuloma as a type IV, T cell mediated reaction.
Recall the loop: macrophages make IL-12, which pushes CD4 T cells toward Th1.
Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages into epithelioid and giant cells.
questions.why: Granulomatous inflammation is a delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity. Antigen-presenting macrophages release IL-12, which drives naive CD4 T cells to become Th1 cells. Th1 cells release IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages into epithelioid cells that may fuse into multinucleated giant cells. TNF from macrophages keeps the granuloma organized, which is why TNF blockers can reactivate latent tuberculosis. Tuberculosis forms caseating granulomas, while sarcoidosis forms noncaseating ones. A tuberculin skin test uses the same pathway and is read as induration at 48 to 72 hours.
whyNot: Correct.

IL-4 drives IgE class switching and alternatively activated macrophages involved in tissue repair. It does not produce the activated, epithelioid macrophages of a Th1 granuloma like those in sarcoidosis.
IL-17 recruits neutrophils and helps defend against extracellular bacteria and fungi. It is not the main driver of granulomas.
IL-10 suppresses macrophage activation and limits inflammation. It works against granuloma formation.

questions.stem: An enlarged hilar lymph node is sampled by endobronchial ultrasound. In a normal lymph node, most lymphocytes entering from the blood cross the vessel wall at which site?
options: Subcapsular sinus, through afferent lymphatics
Medullary sinuses, through the efferent lymphatic
Paracortex, through high endothelial venules
Cortical follicles, through germinal center capillaries
approach: Recall the zones of a lymph node: cortex with follicles, paracortex, and medulla.
Identify the special vessel for lymphocyte entry: the high endothelial venule.
Locate high endothelial venules in the paracortex, the T cell zone.
questions.why: A lymph node has an outer cortex with B cell follicles and germinal centers, a deeper paracortex rich in T cells, and a medulla of cords and sinuses. Lymph enters through afferent lymphatics into the subcapsular sinus and leaves through the efferent lymphatic at the hilum. Blood lymphocytes enter through high endothelial venules in the paracortex, using L-selectin to bind the tall endothelium. T cells stay in the paracortex, and B cells move on to the follicles.
whyNot: Afferent lymphatics carry lymph, dendritic cells, and antigen from tissues into the subcapsular sinus. They are not where blood lymphocytes enter.
The efferent lymphatic is the exit. Lymphocytes leave the node through the medullary sinuses and efferent vessel at the hilum.
Correct.
Follicles hold B cells and germinal centers, but blood lymphocytes do not enter through capillaries there. B cells also enter at the paracortical venules and then move to the follicles.

dx: Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis with scleroderma renal crisis
case: A 44-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of severe headache and blurred vision for 1 day. Over 8 months she has had progressive skin tightening of her fingers, arms, chest, and face, with Raynaud phenomenon, heartburn, and dysphagia. Two weeks ago she began taking prednisone for joint pain. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 204/122 mm Hg. Examination shows thick, bound-down skin from the fingers to the upper arms and over the chest. Serum creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1); it was 0.8 mg/dL 1 month ago. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL (12 to 16), platelet count is 96,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000), and the blood smear shows schistocytes. Anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibodies are positive. Diagnosis: diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis with scleroderma renal crisis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids along with heartburn?
options: Loss of myenteric inhibitory neurons with high sphincter pressure
Smooth muscle fibrosis with low sphincter pressure
Eosinophilic infiltration of the mucosa with esophageal rings
Inflammation of striated muscle in the upper esophagus
approach: Connect skin fibrosis to the same process in the gut wall.
Recall that the lower two-thirds of the esophagus is smooth muscle and is the part affected.
Predict weak peristalsis (dysphagia for solids and liquids) and a weak lower esophageal sphincter (reflux).
questions.why: Systemic sclerosis starts with endothelial injury and autoimmunity. Activated T cells and macrophages release TGF-beta and other mediators that push fibroblasts to lay down excess collagen, while damaged small arteries cause ischemia (Raynaud phenomenon). In the esophagus, the smooth muscle of the lower two-thirds atrophies and is replaced by collagen. Peristalsis weakens and the lower sphincter loses tone, so food sticks and acid refluxes, sometimes leading to Barrett esophagus. The same fibrosis in the lungs causes interstitial lung disease.
whyNot: Loss of inhibitory neurons is achalasia. The sphincter stays tight, which blocks reflux, so heartburn is not a feature.
Correct.
Eosinophilic esophagitis causes food impaction and rings in atopic patients. It does not replace the muscle layer with collagen.
Inflammatory myopathies such as polymyositis weaken the striated upper third and cause trouble starting a swallow, with nasal regurgitation.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of her disease placed her at greatest risk of this renal complication?
options: Raynaud phenomenon present for many years before skin changes
Calcinosis cutis and telangiectasias on the fingers and face
Rapid skin thickening of trunk and proximal limbs
Skin thickening limited to the fingers, hands, and face
approach: Identify the renal crisis: abrupt severe hypertension, rising creatinine, and microangiopathic hemolysis.
Recall that renal crisis occurs mainly in diffuse disease, usually in the first few years.
Pick the feature that defines diffuse disease: rapidly spreading skin thickening proximal to the elbows and onto the trunk.
questions.why: Systemic sclerosis is divided by how far skin thickening spreads. Diffuse cutaneous disease involves skin above the elbows or knees and the trunk, progresses quickly, and brings early visceral disease such as interstitial lung disease and scleroderma renal crisis. It is associated with anti-Scl-70 (and anti-RNA polymerase III) antibodies. Limited cutaneous disease (CREST: calcinosis, Raynaud, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia) stays distal, progresses slowly, carries anticentromere antibodies, and leads to pulmonary hypertension. Glucocorticoids, especially at doses of about 15 mg/day of prednisone or more, also raise the risk of renal crisis, so her recent prednisone matters too.
whyNot: Years of Raynaud before skin changes is the usual course of limited cutaneous disease, which carries a low risk of renal crisis.
Calcinosis and telangiectasia are part of CREST (limited) disease. Its main late visceral threat is pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Correct.
Skin disease distal to the elbows and knees, with or without the face, defines limited cutaneous disease, which rarely causes renal crisis.

questions.stem: At her first visit, before serologic results were available, mixed connective tissue disease was also considered. Which of the following findings would most have supported that diagnosis?
options: High-titer anti-U1 RNP with features of myositis
Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies with rapid skin spread
Antihistone antibodies after starting hydralazine
Anti-dsDNA antibodies with low C3 and C4
approach: Recall that mixed connective tissue disease blends features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis.
Recall the defining serology: high-titer anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein antibodies.
Choose the option that combines this antibody with overlap features such as myositis.
questions.why: Mixed connective tissue disease is an overlap syndrome. Patients typically have Raynaud phenomenon, puffy swollen hands, arthritis, and features borrowed from SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis, such as proximal muscle weakness with a raised creatine kinase. The defining laboratory finding is a high titer of anti-U1 RNP antibodies, usually with a speckled ANA. Her anti-Scl-70 antibodies and widespread skin thickening point instead to diffuse systemic sclerosis.
whyNot: Correct.
Anti-RNA polymerase III marks diffuse systemic sclerosis with a high risk of renal crisis. It would support her final diagnosis.
Antihistone antibodies after hydralazine, procainamide, or isoniazid suggest drug-induced lupus.
Anti-dsDNA with low complement is specific for active systemic lupus erythematosus, often with nephritis.

questions.stem: Her anti-topoisomerase I antibodies are high-affinity, class-switched IgG directed against a nuclear protein. Production of these antibodies most directly requires which of the following?
options: T-independent B cell activation by repeating self epitopes
Cross-reaction of streptococcal M protein antibodies with self
Polyclonal B cell activation by bacterial lipopolysaccharide
Loss of tolerance in autoreactive CD4 helper T cells
approach: Note that the antibodies are high-affinity IgG against a protein antigen.
Recall that class switching and affinity maturation need CD4 T cell help through CD40L and cytokines.
Conclude that self-reactive helper T cells must have escaped central and peripheral tolerance.
questions.why: Self-reactive lymphocytes are normally removed in the thymus and bone marrow (central tolerance) or silenced in the tissues by anergy, regulatory T cells, and deletion (peripheral tolerance). High-affinity IgG against a protein antigen can only form when a B cell gets help from a CD4 T cell that recognizes peptides from the same antigen. So autoreactive helper T cells must escape tolerance, a failure made more likely by HLA susceptibility genes and tissue damage that exposes hidden self antigens. Molecular mimicry, as with streptococcal M protein in rheumatic fever and Campylobacter jejuni in Guillain-Barre syndrome, is another way tolerance can break.
whyNot: T-independent activation by repetitive antigens mainly gives low-affinity IgM. It does not drive class switching and affinity maturation.
Cross-reaction with M protein is the molecular mimicry of rheumatic fever. It does not target topoisomerase I.
Lipopolysaccharide can activate many B cells at once, but this gives mostly low-affinity IgM and no germinal center maturation.
Correct.

topics: T cell help in autoantibody production

case: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of fever and painful joints for 6 days. Pain and swelling began in the right knee, moved to the left ankle, and now involve the right wrist. He had an untreated sore throat about 3 weeks ago. Temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 108/64 mm Hg. Examination shows a swollen, tender right wrist and a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. An ECG shows a PR interval of 0.22 seconds (0.10 to 0.18 for age). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 92 mm/h (0 to 20), C-reactive protein is 8.6 mg/dL (less than 0.5), and the antistreptolysin O titer is 720 Todd units (less than 200). A throat culture is negative. Diagnosis: acute rheumatic fever with carditis.

questions.stem: Endomyocardial tissue from this patient would show Aschoff bodies containing Anitschkow cells. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the injury to his heart?
options: Immune complexes of streptolysin O deposited in the valves
Superantigen-driven polyclonal T cell activation
Antibodies to M protein binding cardiac myosin
Direct invasion of the endocardium by streptococci
approach: Note the 2 to 4 week delay after untreated streptococcal pharyngitis and the sterile inflammation.
Recall that M protein shares epitopes with cardiac myosin and other heart proteins.
Classify the injury as type II hypersensitivity caused by molecular mimicry.
questions.why: Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis by about 2 to 4 weeks. Antibodies and CD4 T cells made against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin, valve tissue, and other self proteins, a type II hypersensitivity reaction driven by molecular mimicry. The result is pancarditis. Aschoff bodies are foci of fibrinoid change with lymphocytes and plasma cells, and Anitschkow cells are activated macrophages with caterpillar-shaped nuclei.
whyNot: Immune complex deposition is a type III mechanism, as in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Rheumatic carditis is driven by cross-reacting antibodies and T cells.
Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins act as superantigens in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, which causes shock within hours, with no delay of weeks.
Correct.
Direct bacterial invasion is infective endocarditis. His throat culture is negative and the injury came weeks after the infection cleared.

questions.stem: If he has recurrent episodes over the next 20 years, which of the following valve lesions is he most likely to develop?
options: Aortic stenosis from calcification of a bicuspid valve
Tricuspid regurgitation from septic vegetations
Mitral prolapse from myxomatous degeneration
Mitral stenosis from commissural fusion
approach: Confirm the diagnosis with the Jones criteria: two major criteria (migratory polyarthritis, carditis) plus evidence of streptococcal infection.
Recall that the acute lesion is mitral regurgitation from valvulitis.
Predict the chronic lesion: repeated attacks scar and fuse the mitral commissures, causing stenosis.
questions.why: The diagnosis rests on evidence of recent streptococcal infection plus two major Jones criteria, or one major and two minor. The major criteria are migratory polyarthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, and Sydenham chorea. Fever, a raised ESR or CRP, and a prolonged PR interval are minor. Acute carditis usually causes mitral regurgitation. Over years, especially with repeat infections, healing leaves thickened leaflets, fused commissures, and short, thick chordae, producing fish-mouth mitral stenosis.
whyNot: A calcified bicuspid aortic valve is a congenital problem that becomes stenotic by middle age. It is not a result of rheumatic fever.
Tricuspid vegetations suggest infective endocarditis in people who inject drugs. Rheumatic disease rarely affects the right-sided valves alone.
Myxomatous degeneration causes floppy leaflets with a midsystolic click, often with connective tissue disorders. It is not a postinflammatory scar.
Correct.

questions.stem: The mechanism that links his sore throat to his heart disease also explains which of the following conditions?
options: Glomerulonephritis 3 weeks after streptococcal impetigo
Guillain-Barre syndrome after Campylobacter enteritis
Polyarteritis nodosa in chronic hepatitis B infection
Toxic shock syndrome from a retained vaginal tampon
approach: Name the mechanism in rheumatic fever: molecular mimicry.
Define it: an immune response to a microbial antigen cross-reacts with a similar host antigen.
Find the option with the same mechanism: Campylobacter lipooligosaccharide mimics peripheral nerve gangliosides.
questions.why: Molecular mimicry happens when a microbe carries an antigen that looks like a host molecule. The immune response that clears the infection then attacks the look-alike self tissue. In rheumatic fever, M protein resembles cardiac myosin. In Guillain-Barre syndrome after Campylobacter jejuni enteritis, antibodies to bacterial lipooligosaccharide cross-react with gangliosides on peripheral nerves, causing ascending paralysis. Other routes to autoimmunity include failed central or peripheral tolerance and HLA susceptibility.
whyNot: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis follows the same organism, but it is caused by immune complexes deposited in glomeruli (type III). No cross-reacting antibody is involved.
Correct.
Hepatitis B associated polyarteritis nodosa is caused by deposits of viral antigen and antibody complexes in vessel walls.
Toxic shock syndrome is caused by TSST-1, a superantigen that activates many T cells at once without any cross-reaction with self.

questions.stem: Which of the following mediators acts directly in the hypothalamus to raise his temperature set point?
options: Prostaglandin E2 made by COX-2
Histamine released by mast cells
Bradykinin cleaved from kininogen
Leukotriene B4 made by neutrophils
approach: Recall that IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha are the pyrogenic cytokines of the acute phase response.
Recall that they induce COX-2 in hypothalamic vessels, producing PGE2.
PGE2 raises the set point, which explains why NSAIDs reduce fever.
questions.why: IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha from activated macrophages drive the acute phase response. In the brain, they induce COX-2 in the vascular endothelium of the hypothalamus, which makes prostaglandin E2. PGE2 acts on neurons in the preoptic area to raise the temperature set point, so the body conserves and makes heat until the new set point is reached. The same cytokines make the liver produce CRP and fibrinogen, which raises his CRP and ESR.
whyNot: Correct.
Histamine causes vasodilation, itching, and edema in type I reactions. It does not reset the hypothalamic thermostat.
Bradykinin increases vascular permeability and causes pain. It is not the final signal for fever.
Leukotriene B4 is made by the lipoxygenase pathway and attracts neutrophils. Fever comes from the cyclooxygenase pathway.

dx: Primary Sjogren syndrome in a mother whose newborn has congenital heart block
case: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician for a postpartum visit. For 2 years she has had a dry mouth, a gritty feeling in both eyes, and intermittent swelling of both parotid glands. A Schirmer test shows 3 mm of wetting in 5 minutes (10 mm or more). Antinuclear antibodies are positive, with anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies, and rheumatoid factor is positive. A labial salivary gland biopsy shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis. Ten days ago she delivered a boy at 38 weeks' gestation whose heart rate was 54/min, and an ECG of the infant showed complete atrioventricular block. Diagnosis: primary Sjogren syndrome in the mother, with congenital heart block in her newborn.

questions.stem: Six years later she develops persistent, firm enlargement of the right parotid gland. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Marginal zone B cell lymphoma of the parotid
Mantle cell lymphoma of the gastrointestinal tract
Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma of the mediastinum
Primary effusion lymphoma of the pleural cavity
approach: Recall that Sjogren syndrome causes chronic lymphocytic infiltration of the salivary glands.
Persistent B cell stimulation in this mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue raises the risk of a clonal B cell tumor.
Name the tumor: extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, often in the parotid.
questions.why: In Sjogren syndrome, CD4 T cells and B cells infiltrate the salivary and lacrimal glands and destroy the acini, causing dry mouth and keratoconjunctivitis sicca. B cells are chronically activated, which shows up as anti-Ro, anti-La, rheumatoid factor, and hypergammaglobulinemia. This ongoing stimulation raises the risk of B cell lymphoma, most often extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the parotid. Persistent unilateral gland enlargement warrants evaluation for lymphoma. Sjogren syndrome can be primary or occur with rheumatoid arthritis or SLE.
whyNot: Correct.
Mantle cell lymphoma comes from naive B cells with a t(11;14) translocation. It is not linked to Sjogren syndrome and does not typically arise in the parotid.
Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma typically presents as a mediastinal mass in young adults and is not driven by chronic salivary inflammation.
Primary effusion lymphoma is linked to HHV-8 in immunosuppressed patients and presents as a body cavity effusion.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional findings is her son most likely to develop during the first weeks of life?
options: Hypocalcemic seizures with an absent thymic shadow
Chorioretinitis with periventricular calcifications
Transient annular erythematous rash of the face
Cataracts with a patent ductus arteriosus
approach: Link the mother's anti-Ro antibodies to neonatal lupus.
Recall that neonatal lupus includes permanent heart block and transient skin, liver, and blood findings.
Predict the annular, light-sensitive rash that fades as maternal antibody is cleared.
questions.why: Anti-Ro (SSA) IgG from a mother with Sjogren syndrome or SLE crosses the placenta and binds fetal tissues. In the fetal heart, it causes inflammation and fibrosis of the conduction system between about 16 and 24 weeks, producing congenital heart block, which is permanent. The same antibodies cause neonatal lupus in the skin: an annular, erythematous rash, often around the eyes and on the face, that appears in the first weeks and fades by about 6 to 8 months as maternal IgG is cleared. Liver enzyme elevation and cytopenias can also occur and are transient.
whyNot: Hypocalcemia with an absent thymus and heart defects is DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion). It is a developmental defect of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.
Chorioretinitis with periventricular calcifications is congenital cytomegalovirus infection.
Correct.
Cataracts, deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus are congenital rubella syndrome.

questions.stem: Her dry mouth also reduces the delivery of secretory IgA to the oral mucosa. In mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, IgA responses begin when which of the following cells carries luminal antigen to the underlying lymphoid follicles?
options: Paneth cells at the base of the crypts
Goblet cells scattered along the villi
Enteroendocrine cells within the crypts
M cells over lymphoid follicles
approach: Recall that secretory IgA is made by plasma cells primed in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.
Identify the cell in the follicle-associated epithelium that samples the lumen.
Name the M cell, which transcytoses antigen to dendritic cells and lymphocytes beneath it.
questions.why: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue includes the tonsils, Peyer patches in the ileum, and scattered follicles in other mucosae. The epithelium over these follicles contains M cells, which take up antigens and microbes from the lumen and pass them to dendritic cells and lymphocytes below. With TGF-beta and T cell help, B cells switch to IgA, then home to mucosae and glands, including the salivary glands. There, plasma cells secrete dimeric IgA joined by J chain, which the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor carries across the epithelium as secretory IgA.
whyNot: Paneth cells sit at the base of small intestinal crypts and secrete defensins and lysozyme. They do not transport antigen.
Goblet cells secrete mucus that forms a barrier over the epithelium. They are not the main antigen-sampling cells of lymphoid follicles.
Enteroendocrine cells release hormones such as cholecystokinin and secretin. They have no role in delivering antigen to lymphoid tissue.
Correct.

questions.stem: The antibody that damaged her son's conduction system reached the fetus in which of the following ways?
options: IgM, which as a pentamer diffuses across the placenta
IgG, carried across the placenta by FcRn
Secretory IgA, carried across by the poly-Ig receptor
IgE, carried to the fetus bound to maternal mast cells
approach: Recall that only one isotype crosses the placenta.
Name the receptor: the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) on syncytiotrophoblast.
Apply it: maternal anti-Ro IgG enters fetal blood and reaches the fetal heart.
questions.why: IgG is the only isotype that crosses the placenta. Syncytiotrophoblast cells take up maternal IgG and move it into fetal blood using the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn), which gives newborns passive protection, and also transfers harmful autoantibodies such as anti-Ro. IgM is the pentameric first-response antibody and the strongest complement activator. Secretory IgA is a dimer in mucosal secretions and breast milk, IgE arms mast cells, and IgD is a receptor on naive B cells.
whyNot: IgM is a large pentamer and cannot cross the placenta. IgM in a newborn means the fetus made it, as in congenital infection.
Correct.
The polymeric immunoglobulin receptor moves IgA across mucosal epithelium into secretions such as breast milk. It does not carry IgA across the placenta.
IgE sits on mast cells and basophils through FcepsilonRI and mediates allergy. It is not transferred to the fetus in any meaningful amount.

dx: Primary (AL) amyloidosis with nephrotic syndrome and restrictive cardiomyopathy
case: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue, leg swelling, shortness of breath on exertion, and foamy urine for 4 months. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg. Examination shows macroglossia with tooth indentations, purpura around both eyes, jugular venous distention, and 3+ pitting edema of both legs. Serum albumin is 2.1 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5), and 24-hour urine protein is 7.8 g (less than 0.15). An ECG shows low voltage. Echocardiography shows thickened ventricular walls, normal-sized ventricular cavities, and impaired diastolic filling. Serum free lambda light chain is 410 mg/L (5.7 to 26.3). A bone marrow biopsy shows 12% clonal lambda-restricted plasma cells. An abdominal fat pad aspirate shows extracellular, amorphous, pink material. Diagnosis: primary (AL) amyloidosis with nephrotic syndrome and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: Which of the following stain findings would confirm the nature of the material in the fat pad aspirate?
options: Magenta staining with periodic acid-Schiff that resists diastase
Blue granular staining with Prussian blue under bright light
Orange-red droplets with oil red O on frozen section
Apple-green birefringence with Congo red under polarized light
approach: Recognize the clinical picture of amyloidosis: nephrotic syndrome, restrictive heart, macroglossia, periorbital purpura.
Recall that amyloid fibrils are proteins folded into cross-beta-pleated sheets.
Apply the stain: Congo red binds the ordered fibrils and shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
questions.why: Amyloid is not one protein. It is any of several misfolded proteins that stack into rigid fibrils with a cross-beta-pleated sheet structure. The fibrils are deposited outside cells, where they resist breakdown and gradually replace normal tissue. Under ordinary light, amyloid is amorphous, glassy, and pink on H&E. Congo red dye lines up along the regular fibrils, so under polarized light the deposits show apple-green birefringence. An abdominal fat pad aspirate is a simple first biopsy site; organ biopsy is used when the fat pad is negative.
whyNot: Diastase-resistant PAS staining marks glycoproteins and mucins, as in alpha1-antitrypsin globules or Whipple disease. It is not specific for amyloid.
Prussian blue stains iron in hemosiderin, as in hemochromatosis or old hemorrhage.
Oil red O stains neutral lipid, as in fatty change. Amyloid is protein and does not take up lipid stains.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional findings is most likely to develop from the same disease process?
options: Numbness of the thumb and index finger at night
Inflammatory back pain with sacroiliac joint fusion
Bronze skin hyperpigmentation with diabetes mellitus
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with anterior uveitis
approach: Identify AL amyloidosis: clonal lambda plasma cells and organ deposits.
List the typical sites of AL deposits: kidney, heart, tongue, skin vessels, peripheral nerves, and the carpal tunnel.
Predict median nerve compression at the wrist, which causes numbness of the thumb and index finger, worse at night.
questions.why: In primary (AL) amyloidosis, a clone of plasma cells secretes excess light chains, more often lambda than kappa. It is a plasma cell dyscrasia and may occur with multiple myeloma. The light chains misfold and deposit in many organs. Glomerular deposits cause nephrotic syndrome. Myocardial deposits stiffen the ventricles and cause restrictive cardiomyopathy with low ECG voltage. Deposits in the tongue cause macroglossia, and fragile vessels in the skin bleed as periorbital purpura. Deposits in the flexor retinaculum compress the median nerve and cause carpal tunnel syndrome, and peripheral and autonomic neuropathy are common.
whyNot: Correct.
Sacroiliac fusion with inflammatory back pain is ankylosing spondylitis. Long-standing ankylosing spondylitis is a cause of AA amyloidosis and has no link to light chain deposits.
Bronze skin with diabetes is hereditary hemochromatosis, which can also cause a cardiomyopathy. Light chain deposits do not cause pigmentation.
Hilar adenopathy with uveitis is sarcoidosis, a granulomatous disease without monoclonal light chains.

questions.stem: The fibrils in his tissues are built mainly from N-terminal fragments of the clonal light chain. Which part of the immunoglobulin molecule do these fragments contain?
options: The heavy chain constant domains that bind Fc receptors
The hinge region joining the Fab arms to the Fc
The variable domain, part of the antigen-binding site
The J chain that links monomers into polymers
approach: Recall the layout of a light chain: one variable domain at the N-terminus and one constant domain at the C-terminus.
Connect the N-terminal fragment to the variable domain.
Recall that the variable domains of the light and heavy chains together form the antigen-binding site in the Fab region.
questions.why: An antibody has two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains joined by disulfide bonds. Each light chain has an N-terminal variable domain and a C-terminal constant domain (kappa or lambda). The variable domains of one light and one heavy chain, with their hypervariable loops, form the antigen-binding site of each Fab arm. The Fc region, made only of heavy chain constant domains, decides isotype functions such as complement fixation and Fc receptor binding. In AL amyloidosis, the unique variable domain sequence of the clone makes the light chain prone to misfold, which is why fibrils are mostly N-terminal variable region fragments.
whyNot: Fc receptor binding comes from the heavy chain constant region, which is not part of a light chain.
The hinge region is part of the heavy chain, between the first and second constant domains. Light chains have no hinge.
Correct.
The J chain is a separate polypeptide that joins IgM pentamers and IgA dimers. It is not part of a light chain.

questions.stem: In a normal lymph node, plasma cells that form after germinal center reactions collect in which region before many of them migrate to the bone marrow?
options: Paracortex around high endothelial venules
Medullary cords near the hilum
Subcapsular sinus beneath the capsule
Mantle zone surrounding germinal centers
approach: Recall that B cells are activated in the follicles and proliferate in germinal centers.
Follow their progeny inward: plasma cells settle in the medulla.
Choose the medullary cords, which lie between the medullary sinuses.
questions.why: In the lymph node cortex, B cells in follicles meet antigen, and with T cell help they form germinal centers, where class switching and affinity maturation take place. Their progeny become plasma cells that move to the medullary cords, strands of tissue between the medullary sinuses near the hilum, where they secrete antibody into the outgoing lymph. Many long-lived plasma cells then travel to the bone marrow. A clone of such marrow plasma cells is the source of the light chains in AL amyloidosis.
whyNot: The paracortex is the T cell zone where lymphocytes enter from the blood. Plasma cells do not gather there.
Correct.
The subcapsular sinus receives lymph from afferent vessels and is lined by macrophages. It is a channel for lymph and does not hold plasma cells.
The mantle zone is a rim of small naive B cells around a germinal center. Its cells are not antibody-secreting plasma cells.

dx: Secondary (AA) amyloidosis with nephrotic syndrome in long-standing ankylosing spondylitis
case: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of swelling of both legs and foamy urine for 3 months. He has a 25-year history of ankylosing spondylitis with persistent back pain despite NSAID treatment. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg. Examination shows reduced lumbar flexion, a fixed thoracic kyphosis, and 3+ pitting edema of both legs. Serum albumin is 2.3 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5), serum creatinine is 1.7 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3), C-reactive protein is 6.4 mg/dL (less than 0.5), and 24-hour urine protein is 6.8 g (less than 0.15). Serum and urine immunofixation show no monoclonal protein. A renal biopsy shows glomerular deposits with apple-green birefringence on Congo red stain that react with antibody to serum amyloid A. Diagnosis: secondary (AA) amyloidosis with nephrotic syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions also carries a risk of this same type of amyloidosis?
options: Multiple myeloma secreting a lambda light chain paraprotein
Familial Mediterranean fever with frequent attacks
Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid gland
Alzheimer disease with cortical neuritic plaques
approach: Identify the amyloid type from the biopsy: serum amyloid A, so AA amyloidosis.
Recall that serum amyloid A is an acute phase protein made by the liver during sustained inflammation.
Pick another condition with long-standing or recurrent systemic inflammation.
questions.why: Secondary (AA) amyloidosis comes from serum amyloid A, an acute phase protein that the liver makes in large amounts under the influence of IL-1, IL-6, and TNF. When inflammation lasts for years, as in rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic infections such as osteomyelitis or tuberculosis, or familial Mediterranean fever, SAA levels stay high. Incomplete breakdown by macrophages leaves AA fragments that form fibrils. The kidney is the main target, and the usual presentation is nephrotic syndrome. Controlling the underlying inflammation lowers SAA and can slow the disease.
whyNot: Myeloma can cause amyloidosis, but its deposits are made of light chains (AL type).
Correct.
Medullary thyroid carcinoma deposits amyloid made from calcitonin locally within the tumor stroma.
Alzheimer plaques contain A-beta amyloid cleaved from amyloid precursor protein. They do not involve serum amyloid A.

questions.stem: His kidney disease progresses, and he receives hemodialysis for 12 years. He then develops bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, shoulder pain with amyloid in the synovium, and cystic lesions of the carpal bones. These new deposits do not react with antibody to serum amyloid A. Which of the following proteins most likely forms them?
options: Transthyretin
Immunoglobulin lambda light chain
Islet amyloid polypeptide
Beta2-microglobulin
approach: Note the setting: long-term hemodialysis.
Recall that beta2-microglobulin, the light chain of MHC class I, is normally filtered by the kidney and is poorly removed by many dialysis membranes.
Match its typical sites: carpal tunnel, synovium, and bone cysts.
questions.why: Different amyloid proteins appear in different settings. Beta2-microglobulin, part of every MHC class I molecule, builds up in patients on long-term dialysis and deposits in joints, tendons, and bone, causing carpal tunnel syndrome and cystic bone lesions. Transthyretin forms amyloid in the hearts of older adults (wild-type) and in hereditary forms. A-beta forms plaques in Alzheimer disease, calcitonin deposits in medullary thyroid carcinoma, and amylin deposits in the islets in type 2 diabetes.
whyNot: Wild-type transthyretin deposits in older adults, mainly in the heart, and can cause carpal tunnel syndrome. It does not explain dialysis-related joint and bone cysts.
Light chain (AL) amyloid needs a plasma cell clone, and his immunofixation found none.
Amylin (islet amyloid polypeptide) deposits in the pancreatic islets in type 2 diabetes.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before his kidney disease began, during a flare of spondylitis with a high CRP, which of the following serum proteins would have been decreased because of the inflammation?
options: Transferrin
Ceruloplasmin
Fibrinogen
Haptoglobin
approach: Recall that IL-6, IL-1, and TNF shift the liver's protein production during inflammation.
Sort proteins into positive acute phase reactants (rise) and negative ones (fall).
Recall that albumin and transferrin are the classic negative acute phase reactants.
questions.why: During the acute phase response, IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-alpha cause hepatocytes to increase production of CRP, serum amyloid A, fibrinogen, haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin, ferritin, and hepcidin. At the same time, the liver makes less albumin and transferrin, the negative acute phase reactants. Lower transferrin and more hepcidin both keep iron away from microbes. The same cytokines also cause fever by raising hypothalamic PGE2.
whyNot: Correct.
Ceruloplasmin is a positive acute phase protein. Its level rises during inflammation.
Fibrinogen rises in inflammation. Its increase makes red cells stack and is the main reason the ESR goes up.
Haptoglobin is a positive acute phase protein and rises during inflammation unless hemolysis is using it up.

questions.stem: His 19-year-old son has 6 months of low back pain and morning stiffness that improve with exercise. The son's inherited risk is most strongly linked to which of the following?
options: HLA-B27, a class II molecule recognized by CD4 T cells
HLA-DR4, a class II molecule recognized by CD4 T cells
HLA-B27, a class I molecule recognized by CD8 T cells
HLA-DR2, a class II molecule recognized by CD4 T cells
approach: Recognize inflammatory back pain in a young man whose father has ankylosing spondylitis.
Recall the HLA association of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies: HLA-B27.
Classify HLA-B as MHC class I, which presents peptides to CD8 T cells.
questions.why: HLA-B27 is strongly linked to ankylosing spondylitis and the other seronegative spondyloarthropathies: reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and arthritis with inflammatory bowel disease. HLA-B27 is an MHC class I molecule, made of a heavy chain paired with beta2-microglobulin, found on all nucleated cells, and recognized by CD8 T cells. Most HLA-B27 carriers never develop disease, so the allele raises risk without being enough on its own.
whyNot: HLA-B is encoded in the class I region. Class II molecules are HLA-DP, -DQ, and -DR, which present to CD4 T cells.
HLA-DR4 is the main susceptibility allele for rheumatoid arthritis, which affects small peripheral joints.
Correct.
HLA-DR2 is associated with multiple sclerosis and Goodpasture syndrome.

topics: MHC class I and class II

dx: Parvovirus B19 transient aplastic crisis in a child with sickle cell disease
case: A 6-year-old boy with homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS) is brought to the emergency department because of increasing fatigue and pallor for 3 days. One week ago he had a low-grade fever and a runny nose. His 8-year-old sister currently has bright red cheeks and a lacy rash on her arms. Temperature is 37.3 °C (99.1 °F), pulse is 138/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 98/58 mm Hg. Examination shows marked pallor, a grade 2/6 systolic flow murmur, and no palpable spleen. Hemoglobin is 3.8 g/dL (his baseline 7.9; reference 11.5 to 14.5), reticulocyte count is 0.2% (his baseline 11%; reference 0.5 to 2.5), leukocyte count is 7,800/mm3 (4,500 to 13,500), and platelet count is 260,000/mm3 (150,000 to 450,000). Serum parvovirus B19 IgM is positive. Diagnosis: transient aplastic crisis caused by parvovirus B19.

questions.stem: His mother is at 20 weeks' gestation and has never been infected with this virus. If she becomes infected, her fetus is at greatest risk of which of the following?
options: Hydrops fetalis from severe fetal anemia
Congenital cataracts with patent ductus arteriosus
Periventricular calcifications with microcephaly
Hydrocephalus with diffuse intracranial calcifications
approach: Recall that parvovirus B19 can cross the placenta.
Note that fetal red cells have short lifespans and the fetus is making red cells rapidly, so halting erythropoiesis causes severe anemia.
Predict high-output heart failure with fluid in body cavities: nonimmune hydrops fetalis.
questions.why: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) in children: a slapped-cheek rash followed by a lacy, reticular rash on the limbs, as in his sister. Adults more often get a symmetric arthropathy. Because the virus stops red cell production, patients who rely on a high red cell turnover, such as those with sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis, can have a sudden transient aplastic crisis. Infection in pregnancy, especially before about 20 weeks, can cause severe fetal anemia, heart failure, and nonimmune hydrops fetalis.
whyNot: Correct.
Cataracts, deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus are congenital rubella syndrome.
Periventricular calcifications with microcephaly and hearing loss are typical of congenital cytomegalovirus infection.
Hydrocephalus, diffuse calcifications, and chorioretinitis are typical of congenital toxoplasmosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following properties of the causative virus best explains the sudden stop in his red cell production?
options: Latent infection of B lymphocytes through CD21
Lytic infection of erythroid precursors bearing P antigen
Infection of CD4 helper T cells using the CCR5 coreceptor
Infection of hepatocytes through the bile acid transporter NTCP
approach: Note the selective drop in reticulocytes with normal white cells and platelets.
Recall that parvovirus B19 binds the P antigen (globoside) on erythroid progenitors.
Apply its lytic replication in these dividing cells: red cell production halts for about 1 to 2 weeks.
questions.why: Parvovirus B19 is a small, nonenveloped, single-stranded DNA virus. It spreads by respiratory droplets, through blood products, and across the placenta. It enters cells through the P blood group antigen (globoside), which is plentiful on erythroid progenitors, and it needs dividing cells to replicate. Infected progenitors are destroyed, so red cell production stops for about 1 to 2 weeks. A healthy person barely notices, but a child with sickle cell disease, whose red cells survive only about 10 to 20 days, quickly becomes severely anemic.
whyNot: Epstein-Barr virus enters B cells through CD21 and establishes latency, causing mononucleosis. It does not selectively stop red cell production.
Correct.
HIV uses CD4 with CCR5 or CXCR4 to infect helper T cells, causing immunodeficiency over years.
Hepatitis B and D viruses enter hepatocytes through the sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP).

questions.stem: His peripheral blood smear is most likely to show which of the following findings that reflects his loss of splenic function?
options: Schistocytes
Basophilic stippling
Teardrop cells
Howell-Jolly bodies
approach: Note the nonpalpable spleen in a 6-year-old with HbSS: repeated infarcts have caused autosplenectomy.
Recall that the spleen normally removes nuclear remnants from red cells as they pass through the red pulp.
Predict persistent nuclear remnants: Howell-Jolly bodies.
questions.why: In sickle cell disease, repeated infarction shrinks the spleen until it no longer works, usually by early childhood. Without splenic function, red cells keep inclusions the spleen would normally pit out, such as Howell-Jolly bodies (small round DNA remnants). Other signs of asplenia are target cells and a raised platelet count. The bigger clinical threat is sepsis from encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis, which is why these children receive vaccines and penicillin prophylaxis.
whyNot: Schistocytes are red cell fragments sheared in small vessels, as in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia or a mechanical valve.
Basophilic stippling is clumped ribosomal RNA, seen in lead poisoning and thalassemia.
Teardrop cells form as red cells squeeze out of a fibrotic marrow, as in myelofibrosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Over years, sickled cells were trapped in his spleen as blood passed through the red pulp, leading to infarction and fibrosis. Which of the following sequences describes the normal path of blood through the spleen?
options: Central artery, venous sinusoids, cords, penicillar arterioles
Penicillar arterioles, central artery, venous sinusoids, cords
Central artery, penicillar arterioles, cords, venous sinusoids
Trabecular artery, cords, penicillar arterioles, venous sinusoids
approach: Start at the hilum: splenic artery to trabecular arteries to central arteries in the white pulp.
Follow the central artery as it branches into penicillar arterioles in the red pulp.
Recall the open circulation: blood empties into the cords, then squeezes through slits into the venous sinusoids and on to the pulp and trabecular veins.
questions.why: Blood enters the spleen through the splenic artery, which branches into trabecular arteries and then central arteries. Each central artery is wrapped in the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath of the white pulp. In the red pulp it divides into penicillar arterioles, most of which empty into the open meshwork of the splenic cords. To return to the circulation, red cells must squeeze through narrow slits between the endothelial cells of the venous sinusoids, then drain into pulp veins, trabecular veins, and the splenic vein. Rigid sickled cells cannot pass these slits, so they pile up in the cords, and repeated congestion leads to infarction and autosplenectomy.
whyNot: This sequence puts the venous sinusoids before the cords. Blood leaves the arterioles into the cords first and only then enters the sinusoids.
The central artery runs through the white pulp before it branches into penicillar arterioles. This order reverses those steps.
Correct.
Trabecular arteries lead into central arteries in the white pulp. They do not open directly into the cords.

dx: Haemophilus influenzae type b epiglottitis in an unvaccinated child
case: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after the sudden onset of high fever and sore throat. She has not received any childhood vaccinations. Temperature is 39.9 °C (103.8 °F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 36/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. She is sitting upright, leaning forward with her neck extended, and drooling. Her voice is muffled, and she has soft inspiratory stridor. A lateral neck radiograph shows a swollen epiglottis (thumb sign). In the operating room, after her airway is secured, the epiglottis appears cherry red and swollen. Blood cultures grow gram-negative coccobacilli. Diagnosis: epiglottitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b.

questions.stem: Her 5-year-old cousin, who is fully vaccinated against this organism, develops acute otitis media, and culture of the middle ear fluid grows Haemophilus influenzae. Which of the following best explains the infection despite vaccination?
options: Antigenic drift in the type b capsular polysaccharide
Cleavage of vaccine-induced serum IgG by IgA protease
Loss of maternal antibody after the first 6 months of life
Infection by a nontypeable strain that lacks a capsule
approach: Recall that the vaccine targets only the type b capsule (polyribosylribitol phosphate).
Recall that most otitis media, sinusitis, and COPD flares due to H influenzae come from nontypeable strains.
Conclude that a strain with no capsule is not covered by the vaccine.
questions.why: Haemophilus influenzae type b, with its polyribosylribitol phosphate (PRP) capsule, causes invasive disease in unvaccinated young children: epiglottitis with drooling and stridor, meningitis, bacteremia, and pneumonia. Since conjugate vaccines came into use, these infections have become rare. Nontypeable strains have no capsule, stay on mucosal surfaces, and cause otitis media, sinusitis, conjunctivitis, and exacerbations of chronic bronchitis. The vaccine raises antibody only to the type b capsule, so it does not prevent these infections.
whyNot: Antigenic drift describes small mutations in influenza virus hemagglutinin and neuraminidase. The type b capsule does not drift.
IgA protease cleaves IgA1 at mucosal surfaces. It does not destroy the serum IgG made by the vaccine.
Maternal antibody fades by about 6 months, but a fully vaccinated 5-year-old has already made antibody against the type b capsule.
Correct.

questions.stem: On sheep blood agar, the organism grows only as tiny colonies next to a streak of Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
options: Need for cysteine and iron supplied by staphylococcal enzymes
Need for reduced oxygen tension created by staphylococcal growth
Need for hemin and NAD released near the staphylococci
Need for carbon dioxide released by staphylococcal metabolism
approach: Recognize satellite growth: Haemophilus colonies cluster around a Staphylococcus aureus streak.
Recall that Haemophilus needs factor X (hemin) and factor V (NAD).
Apply it: S aureus lyses red cells to release hemin and secretes NAD, so both factors are available near the streak.
questions.why: Haemophilus influenzae is a small gram-negative coccobacillus that needs two growth factors: factor X (hemin) and factor V (NAD). Intact sheep red cells hold the hemin, and the agar contains enzymes that break down NAD, so the organism barely grows on plain blood agar. Near a beta-hemolytic Staphylococcus aureus streak, lysed red cells release hemin and the staphylococci secrete NAD, producing satellite colonies. In the laboratory, the organism is grown on chocolate agar, in which heated, lysed red cells supply both factors. Its key virulence factor is the PRP capsule, and it also makes an IgA protease.
whyNot: Cysteine and iron are the growth requirements of Legionella, which is grown on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar.
Needing low oxygen describes microaerophiles such as Campylobacter and Helicobacter. It does not explain growth right next to a staphylococcal streak.
Correct.
Extra carbon dioxide helps Neisseria grow, but it is provided by a CO2 incubator. Haemophilus satellite growth depends on specific growth factors.

questions.stem: The vaccine she did not receive links the type b capsular polysaccharide to a protein carrier. Which of the following best explains why this design protects children younger than 2 years?
options: The polysaccharide cross-links B cell receptors without T cells
Carrier peptides recruit CD4 T cell help for the B cells
The carrier protein activates CD8 cytotoxic T cells against the bacteria
The carrier protein acts as a superantigen on many T cells
approach: Recall that plain polysaccharide is a T-independent antigen and is poorly immunogenic before age 2.
Recall that a B cell specific for PRP takes up the whole conjugate and presents carrier peptides on MHC class II.
Apply T cell help: CD40L and cytokines from CD4 T cells drive class switching, affinity maturation, and memory against PRP.
questions.why: Polysaccharide antigens such as the PRP capsule cannot be presented on MHC, so on their own they activate B cells only by cross-linking their receptors. This T-independent response is weak in children under 2 years, gives mostly IgM, and leaves little memory. In a conjugate vaccine, a B cell that recognizes PRP takes in the whole conjugate and presents peptides from the protein carrier on MHC class II. A carrier-specific CD4 T cell then provides help through CD40L to CD40 and cytokines. That help starts a germinal center reaction, producing high-affinity, class-switched IgG against PRP and long-lived memory.
whyNot: Cross-linking without T cells is the T-independent response to plain polysaccharide. Children under 2 respond poorly to it, and it gives mostly IgM and no memory.
Correct.
Haemophilus is an extracellular bacterium, and protection comes from opsonizing antibody against the capsule. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected host cells.
Superantigens bind outside the peptide groove and activate many T cells at once, causing toxic shock. Vaccine carriers are chosen to avoid this.

topics: T-dependent and T-independent B cell activation

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man who had a splenectomy after a motor vehicle collision is also at increased risk of severe infection with this organism. Loss of which of the following functions most directly accounts for this risk?
options: Removal of opsonized encapsulated bacteria from the blood
Neutrophil oxidative burst killing of catalase-positive bacteria
CD8 cytotoxic T cell killing of virus-infected host cells
Eosinophil major basic protein release against helminths
approach: Note that Hib, like S pneumoniae and N meningitidis, has a polysaccharide capsule that resists phagocytosis.
Recall that the spleen makes IgM against blood-borne polysaccharides in its marginal zone and clears opsonized bacteria in its red pulp.
Predict overwhelming sepsis from encapsulated bacteria after splenectomy.
questions.why: Encapsulated bacteria resist phagocytosis until they are coated with antibody and complement. The spleen is the main place where this happens for organisms in the blood. Marginal zone B cells make rapid IgM against capsular polysaccharides, and macrophages in the red pulp remove the opsonized bacteria. After splenectomy or functional asplenia, these patients can develop overwhelming sepsis from S pneumoniae, Hib, and N meningitidis. Blood smears also show Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, and thrombocytosis.
whyNot: Correct.
A defective oxidative burst is chronic granulomatous disease, which raises the risk of catalase-positive organisms such as S aureus and Aspergillus. Splenectomy does not affect it.
Cytotoxic T cells work in lymph nodes and tissues throughout the body. Splenectomy does not leave a person unusually vulnerable to viruses.
Eosinophils defend against helminths in tissues, a role that does not depend on the spleen.
